$comment: Every way the TypeScript ops and the Python MCP server disagree about which tools exist, what parameters they take and whether they change anything -- one entry each. Result shapes, runtime guards, wording, value constraints, what is inside an object, and every annotation but the read-only hint are outside what the check compares, so they never show up here: a difference can be real and still have no entry, and list_pages carrying no total_matches on the TypeScript side is the standing example. What the check will not do is summarize a construct nobody taught it: it follows no references at all, and a $ref, a $defs, a keyword at the top of an input schema it cannot read, or a composition it does not model stops the run instead of quietly comparing what is left. The parity test fails on a divergence that is not listed here and on a listing the two surfaces no longer support, so this file is the TypeScript to-do list and cannot quietly rot. An entry records that a difference is KNOWN, not that it is fine -- read the status. Statuses: intentional (settled, will not change), pending-port (somebody has read both sides and a TS-side change is owed -- a whole op, or something an existing op still lacks), pending-decision (waiting on a call nobody has made), unreviewed-gap (found by the comparator, nobody has ruled on it yet). What separates pending-port from unreviewed-gap is whether anyone has read both sides, not how serious the difference is: several unreviewed-gap entries describe the same undeclared-default problem as the pending-port ones.

pythonNullDefaults.reason: `x: str | None = None` is how Python spells an optional parameter; the null default carries nothing the TS `.optional()` does not already say.

optionalNullUnions.reason: An OPTIONAL Python parameter typed `T | None` is compared as plain `T`, because that union is how Python spells optional and requiredness is compared separately. A nullable parameter that is required keeps its null, where the union really is part of the contract.

ratchet.$comment: unreviewed-gap is the one status nobody has ruled on, so it is the one meant to go only down. This number is how many of them the registry is allowed to hold: the check fails when there are more, and fails asking for this number to come down when there are fewer, so the count and the number cannot drift apart. What no check can do is stop somebody raising both together -- that edit is in the diff, and refusing it is a reviewer's job. A gap found from here on wants a status somebody reviewed and a reason, not a bigger number.

fixtures.$comment: How much of the surface is compared against the other server at all, which is a different question from how the two surfaces disagree -- so it is counted here rather than as divergence rows. Every tool this server serves answers with a GalaxyResult, and the golden cases under mcp-server-galaxy-py/tests/testdata/envelopes are what that answer is, replayed through the TypeScript MCP server and CLI and compared key for key. A tool with no case is a tool the two can answer differently for ever without anything noticing, which is why the count below is 0 and is held there in both directions: the check fails when an open tool has none, and fails asking for the number to come down when it is above the real count. `excluded` is the short list of tools that may have none, each with the reason; an excluded tool that turns out to HAVE cases fails the check too, so the list cannot outlive what it is excusing.

divergences.observed: python=write (tag) params=[api_key type=string required=false default=none; url type=string required=false default=none]
divergences.reason: TS takes the Galaxy URL and key when the server is built, so there is no per-session connect call to expose.

Both surfaces write the bytes to a local path when they are given one, and both say so; they disagree because the two flags are about different things. Python's read tag is a statement about Galaxy: the tags exist to gate GALAXY_MCP_INCLUDE/EXCLUDE_TAGS, and the tool is two GETs that create, change and delete nothing on the server -- the file Python writes to file_path is outside what the tag speaks to. The MCP readOnlyHint has no such scope: the SDK defines readOnlyHint true as a tool that does not modify its environment, and with filePath the TS op overwrites whatever file is at that path, so it advertises false and clients that gate approval on the hint ask before it runs. Dannon's call (2026-09-26): each flag is correct about its own scope, so neither side moves and the mismatch is what the two scopes look like from the comparator.

builtin.$comment: The third surface: the MCP server Galaxy itself serves (lib/galaxy/webapps/galaxy/api/mcp.py, behind enable_mcp_server), read from the snapshot named in `source`. It calls Galaxy's AgentOperationsManager in process, where the Python tools here go through bioblend and REST and the TypeScript ops through REST -- so the three are three implementations over one Galaxy, not one implementation behind three fronts, and a difference below can sit in either implementation (get_histories' name filter, say, is exact-after-pagination here and name-contains-in-the-query there). This section is kept apart from the python-to-typescript one above on purpose: those two are released together and their ratchet is a promise about this repository, while these rows are a to-do list for a conversation with galaxyproject/galaxy. Same statuses, same rule that an entry the surfaces no longer support fails the check, and its own ratchet, also down-only.
builtin.aliasReason: Two tools with one job and two names, compared under the name this repository uses so their parameters can be compared at all. An alias lines up two SCHEMAS; it is not a claim that the two implementations answer a call alike. list_histories/get_histories both page the current user's histories with limit, offset and a name filter, and agree that far. search_tools/search_tools_by_name both take one `query` string and return matching tools, and that is where the resemblance stops: ours pulls Galaxy's tool index and filters it here for a case-insensitive substring of name, id or description, so `query=""` matches every tool; the built-in hands the query to Galaxy's own toolbox search (`toolbox_search.search` over the default panel view), which is an indexed query parser over more fields than those three and where `query=""` matches nothing. Reconciling those two is a decision about which search an agent should be given, not a rename -- so the schemas are compared here and the behaviour is a reconcile item in the report. Every other name is already shared or is genuinely only on one side -- see the missing-tool rows.

builtinApiKey.reason: Every built-in tool takes a required `api_key` string, because that server authenticates per call; the two surfaces here take the credential once, when the session or the client is built. Comparing it would put the same row on all 44 tools and say nothing about what any of them does. The loader checks the parameter really is there, and required, and a string, on every tool -- so the day one stops taking it, the rule stops the run instead of dropping a parameter nobody looked at.

builtinMutability.reason: The built-in registers every tool with a bare `@mcp.tool()`: no tags, no readOnlyHint, so a client is told nothing about which tools change state and MCP's own default is to assume they all might. That is one real difference from both surfaces here, recorded once rather than as 40 identical rows, and it is a reconcile item for galaxyproject/galaxy rather than something to fix on this side. The loader fails if any built-in tool ever does advertise one, which is when this rule has to be re-decided.

builtinRequirements.reason: A tool served BY a Galaxy cannot need a newer Galaxy than the one serving it, so the built-in declares no version bound and comparing ours against its silence would flag the six Pages tools for a requirement that means nothing there. The loader fails if the built-in ever declares one.

ratchet.$comment: The same down-only counter as above, counted over this section's rows alone. It starts at the number the first run found, because nobody had compared the two surfaces before this one: every row is a difference somebody now has to rule on, and the way the number comes down is a tool changing on one side or somebody reading a row and giving it a reviewed status.

divergences.reason: Ours takes the key as an argument, because connect is the tool that establishes a session; the built-in's api_key is the per-call credential the comparison drops everywhere. So this row is the one place the dropped parameter is a real difference in what the tool does.
Ours points the session at a Galaxy; the built-in is served BY one, so there is no URL to take.

Ours fetches the dataset and can write it to a path on the caller's disk. The built-in returns no bytes at all: its download_dataset hands back a download URL built from galaxy_infrastructure_url, alongside the dataset's name, extension, size and state. So this row is a real difference in what the two tools do rather than a parameter somebody forgot: a server-side tool can point a client at the bytes, and that is all it can do.

Both refuse a dataset that is not ok; only ours can be told not to. AgentOperationsManager.download_dataset returns an error and no download URL whenever the state is anything but `ok`, unconditionally -- so what the built-in is missing is the escape hatch, not the guard. Reconciling this one is a question of whether an agent should ever be able to ask for a dataset that is still running or failed, not of adding a check there.
Ours can name the file after the dataset; Galaxy's has no local file to name.
Both cap the elements returned and the caps differ: 100 here, 500 there.

Ours can put the first N lines of the dataset's text in the answer, read through get_content_as_text; Galaxy's serialises the `detailed` view, which carries `peek` -- the stored few-line snippet Galaxy renders for text-like datatypes -- but no way to ask for the content itself or to leave the peek out.
How many lines ours reads; Galaxy's `peek` is a fixed snippet with no line count to choose.

divergences.observed: builtin=write (mcp default) params=[invocation_id type=string required=true default=none]
divergences.reason: Only Galaxy's. The same reading exists here inside get_invocations, which returns one invocation's detail when it is given invocation_id.
Ours takes an invocation id and returns that one invocation's detail; Galaxy's splits that into get_invocation_details.
Ours declares no default; Galaxy's pages at 50.
Galaxy's pages with limit+offset; ours takes limit only.

Ours can ask for per-step detail on the listing, and Galaxy's server cannot get it at all. get_invocation_details is not the substitute: it builds InvocationSerializationParams(view="element") and leaves step_details at its False default (lib/galaxy/agents/operations.py:617), and a step's jobs, outputs and output_collections are only filled in when the step itself is serialised with view="element" (WorkflowInvocationStep.to_dict, lib/galaxy/model/__init__.py:10917). So what it returns is the invocation's own element view -- state, inputs, input_step_parameters, the invocation's labelled outputs, and a list of steps carrying state, order_index and a bare job_id or implicit_collection_jobs_id -- but no per-step outputs, output_collections or job detail. Ours passes the flag through to the same index endpoint, which serialises the listing with it, so get_invocations(view="element", step_details=True) does return each step's jobs and outputs; and for one invocation by id it sends step_details to GET /api/invocations/{id}, so get_invocations(invocation_id=..., step_details=True) returns each step's jobs too.
Ours chooses how much of each invocation to return; Galaxy's has one shape.

divergences.observed: builtin=write (mcp default) params=[job_id type=string required=true default=none]
divergences.reason: Only Galaxy's, and what it adds is an entry point rather than runtime. get_job_status calls jobs_service.show(full=False) (lib/galaxy/agents/operations.py:318), which is view_show_job -> Job.to_dict("element"): id, state, exit_code, create_time, update_time, tool_id, tool_version, galaxy_version, command_version, history_id, plus params and input/output ids. No runtime and no job metrics -- metrics need full=true and an admin -- and update_time minus create_time is not a runtime, because it includes the time the job sat queued. The gap is the id: a job is reachable here only through get_job_details(dataset_id), which resolves the job from the dataset's provenance and then reads the same non-full job, so an agent holding a job id from run_tool has nowhere to take it.
Galaxy's can return the rendered revision beside the editable one; ours returns the editable text and says which source it came from.
Only here. Galaxy's server has no pre-flight skeleton for run_tool, so an agent there shapes `inputs` from get_tool_details(io_details=True) by hand.

Galaxy's hands the term to WorkflowManager.index_query, which parses it: a bare word matches the name, a tag or the owner, and `name:`/`tag:`/`user:`/`is:` narrow it. A word that appears only in a workflow's annotation is not found. Ours filters name only, through `name`.

divergences.observed: python=read (tag) params=[intent type=string required=true default=none; limit type=integer required=false default=5]
divergences.reason: Only here, and what Galaxy's server is missing is BM25, not free-text ranking as such: its search_iwc_workflows takes a natural-language query -- its own examples are sentences -- and ranks the manifest through iwc.search_workflows. That score is a count (lib/galaxy/agents/iwc.py:155): one point per query token found anywhere in name, annotation, tags, the 300-character readme summary and tool names, with no IDF, no term frequency and no length normalisation, so a common word weighs as much as a rare one and integer ties are ordinary. Ours scores with rank_bm25's Okapi over name (counted twice, to weight it), annotation, tags, the whole readme and tool names, minus a stop-word list, so a rare term separates workflows a token count ties and a long readme does not win for being long. It is not one-way: ours tokenises runs of two or more letters, so a term like hg38 tokenises to nothing, where Galaxy's alphanumeric tokeniser keeps it. Both drop zero scores and return match_score.

Ours can ask for a specific tool version (posted through to Galaxy, which may still fall back to an installed one); Galaxy's runs whatever version the toolbox resolves for the id and takes no version.
Both cap the ranking and the caps differ: 20 here, 10 there.
Ours pages the results; Galaxy's returns the top `limit` and no more.
